h1: Brewing a coffee stout at home with cold brew coffee
title: Coffee Stout With Cold Brew Coffee | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew a coffee stout with cold brew: which beans to choose, how to make the concentrate and how to dose it into 20 litres by taste.
teaser: Cold brew gives a coffee stout fresh aroma without harsh bitterness. The dosing is where most homebrewers go wrong.
standfirst: Coffee and stout already share roast and bitterness. Cold brew concentrate adds fresh coffee aroma without the harsh, acrid edge of hot coffee. Added at packaging and dosed by taste, it is the easiest coffee method to control.
sections: Cold brew is gentler than hot coffee

Hot coffee added to beer brings bitterness and astringency on top of what the roasted malt already gives. It also fades and stales quickly. Cold brew is steeped in cold water for many hours, so it extracts aroma and sweetness but fewer of the harsh compounds. The result tastes rounder in beer and holds its aroma longer.

It also keeps coffee oils low. Oils damage foam, so a coffee stout made with cold brew holds a better head than one made with espresso.
Start with a stout that can carry it

Coffee works in most stouts. A dry stout gives a lean, roasty result. An oatmeal or sweet stout gives a rounder, mocha-like beer. For a first attempt, we would pick an oatmeal stout at around 1.055 to 1.060 and 5.5 to 6% ABV with 30 to 35 IBU. Lower bitterness leaves room for the coffee.

Our basic stout guide covers the brew day. Nothing changes there: the coffee goes in at the end.

India grows both arabica and robusta, mainly in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. For beer:

  • A medium roast arabica gives chocolate, nut and some fruit
  • A dark roast adds more roast but can taste ashy alongside roasted barley
  • Robusta brings strong body and more bitterness, best used in a blend

Avoid filter coffee powder blended with chicory. Chicory adds a woody bitterness and the fine grind clogs everything. Buy whole beans and grind coarse, like rough sugar, just before steeping.

A simple method for a 20 litre batch:

  1. Boil 1 litre of water and let it cool to room temperature. Boiling sanitises it.
  2. Add 150 to 200 g of coarsely ground coffee to a clean jar and pour in the water.
  3. Stir, seal and refrigerate for 18 to 24 hours.
  4. Strain through a sanitised fine mesh, then a paper coffee filter.

That gives roughly 700 to 800 mL of concentrate, since the grounds hold back some water. Keep it sealed in the fridge and use it within a day or two. The concentrate is not sterile, so handle it with the same care as any cold-side addition.

Coffee strength varies with bean, roast and grind, so a fixed recipe dose is a guess. Pour 200 mL of finished, flat stout into three glasses. Add 3 mL, 5 mL and 8 mL of concentrate with a syringe. Taste them. If the 5 mL glass is right, scale up: 5 mL in 200 mL is 500 mL in 20 litres.

Most brewers land between 250 and 600 mL of concentrate for 20 litres. Go slightly below what tastes perfect in the flat sample. Carbonation and cold serving both lift coffee aroma.
Add it at packaging, then chill

Add the measured concentrate to the keg or bottling bucket and rack the beer onto it, so it mixes without splashing. Adding coffee during active fermentation drives off aroma with the CO2 and wastes good beans.

Cold crashing before packaging clears the stout and drops yeast. Our guide to cold crashing without suck-back covers the airlock problem that pulls sanitiser into the beer. Carbonate to about 2.0 to 2.3 volumes and drink within two or three months. Coffee aroma fades faster than the stout itself, especially in warm storage.

Green, grassy or vegetal coffee notes often mean the coffee was steeped too long or contains underdeveloped beans. Harsh bitterness usually means too fine a grind. Sourness in the finished beer can mean the concentrate picked up bacteria. Separating these from roasted malt faults is a palate skill. It is also a common reason homebrewers enter a style course.

Coffee beer carries caffeine. A pint of coffee stout dosed at 500 mL of concentrate per 20 litres contains noticeably less caffeine than a cup of filter coffee, but it is not zero. Mention coffee clearly on the label or the tap list so anyone avoiding caffeine knows. Decaf beans work well if you want to serve the beer late in the evening. Choose a decaf roasted for espresso, which tends to keep more body.

Storage matters for aroma. Keep kegs and bottles cold, ideally below 8 °C, from the day you package. A coffee stout left on a warm shelf for a month loses its fresh coffee note first, then picks up a stale, papery edge. Brew a batch size you can finish while it still smells like the roaster's bag.
Find your dose in a shop-bought stout

Buy 250 g of whole medium roast arabica from a local roaster and make a 500 mL test batch of cold brew this week. Add it to a commercial stout by the glass using a syringe. You will learn your preferred dose before your own stout is even brewed.
faqs: How much cold brew goes into 20 litres of stout?
Most brewers use 250 to 600 mL of concentrate. Find your dose by bench testing small samples first.
When should I add coffee to beer?
At packaging. Adding it during fermentation drives off aroma with the escaping CO2.
Can I use South Indian filter coffee?
Avoid blends with chicory and fine grinds. Use whole beans ground coarse.
